cognate: Gk εὐμενής = Ved. sumánas- (Av. humanah-), exact compound *h₁su-menes- 'of good mind, well-disposed'
drift_or_renewal: Greek pairs it with ἵλαος 'appeased, gracious' (ἵλεως καὶ εὐμενεῖς), Vedic with á-heḷant 'not angry' (sumánāḥ áheḷan, RV 1.91.4c, 10.32.8d): the second member is renewed, the figure ('well-minded and not wrathful') kept. Avestan humanah- has drifted to the human ethical triad (humanah-/huvacah-/hušiiaoϑna-), not used of gods
shared_syntax: predicative/attributive adjective of a deity (or the gods) whose favour the worshipper asks: Ved. sumánāḥ bhava/astu/upā́gahi 'be/come well-minded (to us)'; Gk θεοὺς ... εὐμενεῖς εἶναι, γενοῦ ... εὐμενής, θεοὶ ... ἵλεως καὶ εὐμενεῖς (πέμπειν)
context: Prayer or sacrifice before an undertaking: Cyrus prays to the gods and heroes of Persis to send the army off propitious and well-minded (Cyr. 2.1.1), sacrifices to the gods he thought propitious and well-minded (3.3.21); Hell. 6.4.2 the gods 'most well-minded'. In the RV sumánas- is a stock epithet (32 padas) of Agni, Indra etc. in requests for favour, often with imperative 'be' or 'come'; Greek tragedy and the Homeric Hymn to Poseidon use εὐμενής the same way in prayers. Same referent class, same speech act, exact compound: the match is not mere co-occurrence of 'good' and 'mind'

cognate: Ved. dyáuḥ pitā́ = Gk Ζεῦ πάτερ / Ζεὺς πατήρ = Lat. Iū-piter (*dyēu ph₂tēr), sky-god + 'father'
drift_or_renewal: The Greek slab anchor has the derivative πατρῷος 'ancestral, of the fathers' (Ζεὺς πατρῷος, a cult title, also applied to Hestia) instead of πατήρ itself; Homer keeps Ζεῦ πάτερ / Διὶ πατρί (support). In Cato the sky-god appears as Iou- (oblique of the univerbated Iuppiter) and pater is transferred to Mars in the same prayer (Mars pater ... precor), the Italic 'god + pater' address type
shared_syntax: divine name *dyēu- in apposition with (or qualified by) *ph₂tēr, as an address or designation in prayer/hymn
context: All in religious speech: AV hymns to plants name Dyaus the father and Earth the mother of the herbs; Cyrus prays to Hestia patroa and Zeus patroos before setting out on campaign; Cato's lustration prayer opens with libation to Janus and Jupiter and invokes Mars pater. The formula is too specific (named sky-god + kin term 'father') to be generic, but in this slab it is carried only in drifted Greek and split Latin form

cognate: *péḱu 'cattle' (Lat. pecua; Ved. paśú-, Av. pasu-, Umbr. pequo in support) in the merism *wiHro- peḱu 'men and cattle'
drift_or_renewal: renewal in both slab anchors: Latin pastores replaces *wiHro- (Umbrian keeps ueiro pequo, with saluo seritu = Cato salua seruassis); the AV verse renews both members (go- 'cows' for paśu-, puruṣa- for vīra-), keeping the frame 'welfare (svasti ~ salus) for family, cattle and men'. The cognate pair itself appears only in support (AVP paśubhiś ca vīraiḥ, Av. pasuuā̊ vīraiiā̊)
shared_syntax: coordinated men + cattle as beneficiaries (dative / object) of a protection-welfare request addressed to gods, alongside the household (Lat. domo ... familiae ~ Ved. mātra ... pitre)
context: Both are prayers for the safety of a household: Cato's lustration prayer to Mars asks that he keep safe herdsmen and herds and give good health to master, house and household; the AV verse asks well-being for mother and father, for cows, for the moving world and for men. The Umbrian and Avestan prayers carry the same merism with the inherited words. Weak as anchored here, since neither slab passage keeps both inherited members, and men-and-cattle prayers could arise among any herders
phrase: *wiHro- peḱu 'men and cattle' kept safe (Lat. salua seruare, Umbr. saluo seritu, Av. ϑrāϑrāi)

cognate: *swoyd-/*sweyd- 'sweat' (Gk ἱδρώς, ἱδρόω; Ved. svéda-, svid-) together with *ḱemh₂- 'toil, tire' (Gk κάματος, κάμνω; Ved. śam-, śámī-) in support
drift_or_renewal: none in the sweat member; the Xenophon anchor has only the noun ἱδρῶτα as object of 'provide', not the figura or the toil word
shared_syntax: figura etymologica cognate object + cognate verb: Ved. svédam āsiṣvidānā́ 'having sweated sweat' = Hom. ἱδρῶ ... ἵδρωσα 'the sweat I sweated'; and sweat coordinated with or attached to *ḱemh₂- toil (Hom. κάματός τε καὶ ἱδρώς; Ved. śaśamānásya ... svédasya, śámīm śaśamānás ... siṣvidānáḥ)
context: Sweat as the mark of hard labour: Cyrus takes his men hunting so they sweat (Xen.); the Aśvins are compared to ploughmen who have sweated sweat (RV 10.106.10); Hera's sweat sweated in toil, her horses tired out (Il. 4.27); the toiling, sweating worshipper whom the Maruts should heed (RV 1.86.8, 5.42.10). The two cognate roots in the same toil-and-sweat setting in both Greek and Vedic make it more than chance, but the association is a natural one and the slab anchors carry only the sweat word
